plan.analysis: The constant seed attains 2/3, but a simple symmetric three-step tent [1,2,1] already gives R≈0.6736 by hand, and optimizing [1,c,1] gives ≈0.6778 near c≈1.65. So 2/3 is not the optimum. I am betting the best lower bound is a smooth symmetric unimodal step profile, with a possible asymmetric or multi-modal correction. The experiments test short symmetric families exactly, refine a fine symmetric profile by local optimization, and probe asymmetry/multi-modality by simulated annealing.

experiments.change: Search symmetric step arrays for N in {3,5,7,9}. For each N use variables h_0..h_floor((N-1)/2) with the mirror symmetry h_i=h_{N-1-i}; parameterize h_i=exp(u_i) and normalize the mean height to 1 inside the objective. Objective is -R(h), with R computed exactly from L=[0,*np.convolve(h,h),0] using the given formula. Use scipy.optimize.minimize(method='Nelder-Mead') from multiple starts: all-ones, the embedded tent [1,1.65,1], and 10 random log-normal perturbations. Keep the global best, loop over N/restarts until time.process_time() reaches 0.9*budget, and return the best heights (also comparing with start).
experiments.prediction: Best R will be strictly above 0.666667, around 0.677-0.680; increasing N beyond 3 may give a small additional gain.

experiments.hypothesis: A fine symmetric unimodal tent, with heights allowed to vary smoothly over many steps, will improve on the short three-step tent.

plan.analysis: The evidence is that higher R comes from flatter f*f tops (F6), and the algebra says why: if g=f*f is nearly constant, R≈1. The classic near-extremal choice is f(x)∝x^{-1/2} (or symmetric (x(1-x))^{-1/2}), whose autoconvolution is exactly constant on half the support; discretizing f_i∝(i+1/2)^{-1/2} with a finite end height should already give R≈0.90, well above 0.865. So the biggest expected gain is to change the shape family from a Gaussian bump to an endpoint-singular power law, then polish it. I bet on a singular left edge (asymmetric, consistent with F3/F6) plus a smooth modulation optimizing the decaying tail.

experiments.hypothesis: The Gaussian-bump seed is the wrong family; a discretized Beta/power singularity x^{-p} at one end makes f*f nearly constant on most of the support, so R should jump far above 0.865.
experiments.change: Replace the bump seeding block: for n in (200,400,800) and p in (0.35,0.5,0.65,0.8), build h_i = ((i+0.5)/n)^(-p), also a mirrored/right-singular version and a symmetric ((i+0.5)(n-i-0.5)/n^2)^(-p) version, clip the largest height to 1e3, evaluate exact R, keep the best; then run the existing hill-climbing/smoothing loop from that seed (still accepting the incoming `start` if better). Keep the deadline logic.
experiments.prediction: Best R ≥ 0.88, with p≈0.5 winning, confirming the x^{-1/2} mechanism; the reported profile will have max/mean ≫ 3.5 and one very tall edge step.

experiments.hypothesis: The optimal shape is a smooth modulation on top of a near-singular edge; a low-dimensional parametric family fitted directly will beat blind hill-climbing and reveal the tail shape.
experiments.change: At N=2000 build h_i = ((i+0.5)/N)^(-0.5) * exp(c0 + c1*u + c2*u^2 + c3*u^3 + c4*u^4) with u=(i+0.5)/N (5 coefficients), plus optional floor t: h = h + t. experiments.prediction: Fitted R at least 0.90, with the optimal modulation bending the tail upward (not pure x^{-1/2}) and t>0; the gain over experiment 1 shows the interior modulation matters.

plan.analysis: p0012 (0.8808) is essentially x^{-1/2} times a mild quartic modulation, i.e. the algebraically predicted flat-autoconvolution edge, but it falls ~0.02 short of the ~0.90 algebra bound (F12). The three candidate causes are: the fixed exponent/degree-4 modulation is too stiff, finite-N quadrature, or the single-edge ansatz is structurally wrong. I bet on stiffness first (richer family, multi-N), then on a genuinely different search (free-form gradient in log-height space from p0012's basin, which p0013 never tried), and finally on a different structure (singularities at both ends) to test whether the single-edge mechanism is really optimal.

experiments.hypothesis: The 0.8808 plateau is caused by the family being too stiff: fixed exponent -0.5 and only a quartic log-modulation cannot bend the tail enough to shrink the f*f decay on [1,2]. A free exponent plus a degree-8 modulation, fitted at moderate N and re-scored at high N, will find a better tail.
experiments.change: In p0012's _build use params = (p, c0..c8, t): u=(i+0.5)/N; h = u**(-p) * exp(clip(sum_{k=0..8} c_k u**k, -60, 60)) + max(t,0), with p clipped to [0.05,1.5]. Fit at N=1200 with Nelder-Mead (maxfev 8000) then L-BFGS-B, multi-start from (a) p=0.5 plus a degree-8 polyfit of log(start*sqrt(u)) vs u, t=0, (b) p in {0.35,0.5,0.65}, zero poly, t=1e-3, (c) 0.05-scale random perturbations of the incumbent, restarting until 0.85*budget. Then rebuild the best params at N in {2000,4000,8000}, score each with _R, and return the best-scoring array (also compare the incoming start). Print best p, best R per N.
experiments.prediction: R >= 0.885 at some N; the optimum has p clearly different from 0.5 and nonzero c5..c8, confirming family stiffness (F12); if R stays <= 0.882 the family is not the bottleneck.

experiments.hypothesis: Any low-dimensional ansatz is the bottleneck. Directly optimizing all N heights in log-space, started inside p0012's singular-edge basin (never done: p0013's gradient run started from the Gaussian-bump basin), with an exact analytic gradient and FFT convolution, will escape the parametric family and push R toward the algebra bound.
experiments.change: Resample the incoming start (p0012's array) to N=2000 by linear interpolation, set y=log(h+1e-6). Minimize -R(exp(y)) with scipy L-BFGS-B using the analytic gradient: L=fftconvolve(h,h); S=h.sum(); num=(sum L^2 + sum L[:-1]*L[1:])/3; M=L.max(); den=S*S*M; g_j = (2L_j + L_{j-1} + L_{j+1})/3 - (num/den)*S*S*[j==argmax(L)] (zero-padded boundaries); grad_h = 2*correlate(g,h) implemented as np.convolve(g, h[::-1]) with the correct slice; grad_y = grad_h*h. Verify grad_y against finite differences at N=20 before the run. Optimize at N=2000 until 0.6*budget, then linearly upsample h to N=4000 and continue L-BFGS-B until 0.9*budget; return the best array over both resolutions and the start.
experiments.prediction: R >= 0.890, beating p0012 by >=0.009 and showing the parametric family was the limiter; if it stalls at <=0.882 the x^{-1/2} algebra bound is loose rather than the family.

experiments.hypothesis: The single left-edge singularity leaves a decaying f*f tail on the right half; adding a second, weaker singularity at the right end can flatten that tail and raise R. A two-edge power family nests the pure x^{-1/2} case, so it directly tests whether the one-sided mechanism is optimal.

plan.analysis: The singular-edge basin is locally saturated: four independent attacks on p0012 (richer family, free-form gradient, two-edge, multi-resolution) all land at 0.8808-0.8816, and p0015 (best, 0.881554) used only 8.3 s of its 30 s budget. p0019 reaches the same 0.881554 from a genuinely different shape (f*f peak at 0.364 vs p0015's 0.057), so the 0.8816 plateau may be a local max of the free-form problem, not the global one. Three untested levers: (a) a vanishing-right-edge family u^{-p}(1-u)^{+q}, which predicts a steeper f*f tail y^{1+2q} than the jump edge; (b) actually spending the full budget on randomized restarts; (c) resolving the singular edge with N=10000-20000, since the discrete score rewards a better-resolved spike (F18's open quadrature question). I bet modest gains (+0.001-0.004) live in one of the resolution/restart levers, and the structural (1-u)^q test settles the tail question.

experiments.hypothesis: p0019's two-edge shape ties p0015 at 0.881554 but sits in a different region (f*f peak at 0.364 vs 0.057), so its basin was never freely optimized. Also, a right edge that *vanishes* like (1-u)^q makes f*f decay as y^{1+2q} at x=2 (steeper than the linear jump-edge tail), which should raise R if the tail is the loss.

Two untested levers remain: (i) the anneal is proposal-starved (~300 descents in 30 s) because each full L-BFGS descent at N=20000-40000 is expensive — a coarse 42-dim basis makes descents ~5x cheaper, enabling a far more thorough ridge walk; (ii) nobody has run a true global optimizer over the physically-motivated two-exponent singular family, so F54's 'global optimum' claim is unverified. I bet one of these breaks the plateau; the third experiment squeezes p0058's strongest line by extending smoothing to global scales.

experiments.hypothesis: The Metropolis anneal (F43) was the only mechanism to gain, but at N=20000-40000 each full L-BFGS descent costs ~0.1 s, so only ~300 proposals fit in 30 s. Representing log h in a 42-dim basis (two free edge exponents a,b plus 40 Chebyshev modes) makes each descent ~20 ms, allowing 1000+ proposals to explore the ridge far more thoroughly; mapping the best coefficient vector back to full N and free-form polishing should then beat the current point.

Project c0 = lstsq(B, log(max(start,1e-9))). Define _negR_grad_c(c): h=exp(clip(B@c,-30,30)); R,gh=_R_grad(h); dRdy=gh*h; return -R, -(B.T@dRdy). Run a Metropolis-over-local-optima anneal in c-space for ~0.7*budget (T geometric 2e-5->1e-7, proposal N(0,0.05) on c, full L-BFGS on the 42-dim objective each proposal, accept worse with prob exp(dR/T), record best-by-exact-R). Map best c to h at N=len(start), then run p0058's _optimize (free-form log-space L-BFGS) on it until 0.90*budget. Return the better by exact R of {start, coarse-anneal result}.
experiments.prediction: If the ridge is a coarse shape feature, coarse anneal finds R >= 0.88205 (+3e-5); if the gain needs fine detail or the ridge is already fully explored, it returns <= 0.882024.

experiments.hypothesis: F54's claim that 0.882 is a global optimum rests only on local descents from one basin. experiments.prediction: If a better basin exists in this family, some DE point polishes to R > 0.88205; if all top-5 polish back to <= 0.882024, the family's global optimum is the current point, confirming F54.

plan.analysis: p0062 (+0.000103) is the only real break above 0.882024, and its signature is a *smoother* profile: max/mean fell 34.4 -> 29.2 and the f*f 1%-share rose to 49.62%. So the gain came from denoising the ridge, not from finer resolution — F58/F64 (smoothing at N=40000) failed while the 20000->40000->20000 round trip worked. I bet on pushing that mechanism: (a) iterate the whole smooth/upsample/downsample/polish cycle instead of running it once, (b) test whether an even smoother low-N basin upsamples to a better point, (c) replace midpoint downsampling with block-mean denoising.

experiments.hypothesis: The multiscale-smooth + upsample + downsample + polish cycle gained +1e-4 in a single pass; it is a contraction toward a smoother ridge point and has not been iterated, so repeated passes should keep finding small gains until the deadline.
experiments.change: In construct, after loading start, wrap stages 1-3 in a loop: while time.process_time() < 0.85*budget: (i) run _refine_multiscale at current N for a fixed ~4 s slice, (ii) upsample to min(2N, 60000), L-BFGS polish, (iii) downsample back to N=20000 via _upsample_preserve, L-BFGS polish, (iv) keep best-by-exact-R globally. Reserve the last ~15% of budget for a single tight L-BFGS polish of the best-ever h at N=20000 (maxiter 5000, no kicks). Log R after each pass.
experiments.prediction: Each extra pass adds 1e-5 to 5e-5; total >= 0.88215. If passes 2+ add < 5e-6, the one-pass gain was a one-off and the mechanism is exhausted.

experiments.hypothesis: If the limiting structure is genuinely smooth (max/mean dropped to 29.2, 1%-share rose), then the high-frequency detail at N=20000/40000 is noise; optimizing the shape at a much lower resolution should land in a better basin that survives upsampling.

plan.analysis: Recent gains are ~1e-5 and come from low-pass contraction of one smooth ridge (F61/F67/F68/F73); spline reparametrization (F75), pure high-N freedom (F70/F72) and anneal diversity (F49/F56/F60) add nothing. p0078's independent lineage reached 0.882173 in gen 13 by the same multiscale mechanism on a different basin whose f*f top is equally flat but lower-peaked, so near-optima look nearly degenerate. I bet on: (1) making acceptance resolution-consistent (p0077 currently compares R values measured at N=5000, 40000, 80000 and 20000 as if they were the same number); (2) transplanting the block-mean/low-N machinery onto p0078's fresh basin; (3) a direct test of whether the returned step count itself biases the exact R, which nobody has measured.

experiments.hypothesis: p0077 adopts a new candidate whenever its R measured at the candidate's own N beats best_R, but best_R mixes values measured at N=5000, 40000, 80000 and 20000; R_N is the exact score of a step function, so these numbers are not comparable and a 40000-step candidate that looks better may block-mean down to a worse 20000-step array. Scoring every candidate at the fixed output resolution N=20000 should recover some of that loss and make the keep-best logic monotone in the quantity actually graded.
experiments.change: In p0077's construct, keep the identical stage schedule and optimizers, but change only the acceptance rule: maintain a single best_h20 (length 20000) and best_R20 = _R(best_h20) from the start (block-mean downsample the start to 20000 if needed). Whenever a candidate hb of length n is produced (5000, 40000 or 80000), form hb20 = _block_downsample(hb, 20000) if n is a multiple of 20000, else _resample(hb, 20000) (for n<20000 use _resample to up to 20000), and adopt it only if _R(hb20) > best_R20. Always return best_h20 (length 20000), after a final tight L-BFGS polish at N=20000 until 0.92*budget. Print, each time a candidate is rejected, the pair (R at its own n, R at 20000) so the number of cross-resolution flips is logged.
experiments.prediction: Final R >= 0.882233 (+8e-6 over p0077), and the log shows at least a few candidates with higher R at 40000/80000 than at 20000 that were previously adopted — i.e. cross-resolution flips are the source of the gain. If final R <= 0.882226 the mixed-N bookkeeping was harmless and the remaining plateau is not an acceptance artifact.

experiments.hypothesis: p0078 gained +2.1e-4 (the largest gen-13 gain) from p0035's basin using a multiscale loop plus one N=40000 intermediate polish, but it never got the block-mean downsample (F68) or coarse-first (F69) stages that were worth +8.6e-5 and +4.4e-5 on the p0062 branch. plan.analysis: The singular-basin line (p0089→p0095) sits at 0.882421, still 1.2e-4 below the continuous x^-1/2 bound 4ln2/pi=0.882542. F96/F94 rule out first-cell quadrature, exponent, and smooth modulation; the wall looks like the hard max over a flat top whose wiggle knots are individually peaked (gradient only pushes down one knot). Best remaining bets: (a) smooth the max so the whole flat top rises together; (b) push N far higher than 40k to test whether the wall is finite-N flat-top discretization; (c) test a genuinely different two-sided singular basin. All wrap in keep-best-by-exact-R so downside is zero.

experiments.hypothesis: The hard argmax in _R_grad gives signal from one knot, so the flat top of x^-1/2's f*f stays wiggly and cannot jointly rise. Replacing the argmax with a top-k mean (softmax-style) distributes gradient over the whole flat region, letting L-BFGS flatten and raise the top, which should translate to a higher true R after exact re-scoring.
experiments.change: In p0095's _R_grad, add a flag softmax_k=500. When set, compute L, find the k=int(502) largest knots via np.argpartition, replace M=argmax with Ms=L[topk].mean() and replace the single-knot term dR_dL[imax] -= (num/den)/M with dR_dL[topk] -= (num/(s*s*Ms)) / k (chain-rule of den=s²·mean-top-k). Keep _R (exact, hard max) as the accept criterion. In construct, replace _negR_grad with a softmax version and run p0095's full pipeline unchanged for ~70% of the budget (softmax throughout the L-BFGS calls), then do the last ~20% as a hard-max polish from the best-by-exact-R array. Print every accepted R.
experiments.prediction: Score strictly exceeds 0.882421 (+1e-5 to +1e-4); if the flat top is the bottleneck, the accepted arrays show reduced knot-wiggle in L and R climbs toward 0.88250. If softmax gains nothing (R=start), the hard-max gradient is not the blocker.

Also evaluate the 'sum' variant h[i]=(i+0.5)^-0.5+(N-i-0.5)^-0.5 and the plain x^-1/2 seed; pick the one with highest exact _R, print all three, then run p0095's pipeline (N=40000 refinement + final N=20000 polish), keeping best-by-exact-R. Return best_h20.
experiments.prediction: If a two-sided basin beats 0.882421, we have a new candidate shape; if the best is still the one-sided x^-1/2 seed and final R≤0.882421, then x^-1/2 is confirmed locally optimal in the singular family and one-sidedness is not the missing 1.2e-4.

experiments.hypothesis: The hard argmax in _R_grad gives signal from one knot, so the flat top of x^-1/2's f*f stays wiggly and cannot jointly rise. Replacing the argmax with a top-k mean (softmax-style) distributes gradient over the whole flat region, letting L-BFGS flatten and raise the top, which should translate to a higher true R after exact re-scoring.
experiments.change: In p0095's _R_grad, add a flag softmax_k=500. When set, compute L, find the k=int(502) largest knots via np.argpartition, replace M=argmax with Ms=L[topk].mean() and replace the single-knot term dR_dL[imax] -= (num/den)/M with dR_dL[topk] -= (num/(s*s*Ms)) / k (chain-rule of den=s²·mean-top-k). Keep _R (exact, hard max) as the accept criterion. In construct, replace _negR_grad with a softmax version and run p0095's full pipeline unchanged for ~70% of the budget (softmax throughout the L-BFGS calls), then do the last ~20% as a hard-max polish from the best-by-exact-R array. Print every accepted R.
experiments.prediction: Score strictly exceeds 0.882421 (+1e-5 to +1e-4); if the flat top is the bottleneck, the accepted arrays show reduced knot-wiggle in L and R climbs toward 0.88250. If softmax gains nothing (R=start), the hard-max gradient is not the blocker.

experiments.hypothesis: p0097 only tested N=40000 with the exact cell-average seed and got 0.882396 from the SAME starting basin, leaving the 1.2e-4 wall essentially unchanged. If the wall is finite-N discretization of the flat interior of f*f (F96's open question), going to N=200000 should visibly shrink it, even without heavy optimization.
experiments.change: In p0095's construct, set N20=Nmid=200000. Seed best_h with the exact cell-average singular profile h[i]=2*sqrt(N)*(sqrt(i+1)-sqrt(i)), i=0..N-1, at N=200000. Compute and print exact _R of this raw seed. Then run at most a short p0095-style L-BFGS phase (maxiter=300, log-space, keep-best-by-exact-R), leaving the rest of the budget unused only if the raw seed already beats everything (return best). Return the N=200000 array.
experiments.prediction: If the wall is finite-N flat-top discretization, the raw seed's exact-R at N=200000 is notably higher than 0.882396 (possibly approaching 0.88250), and final R > 0.882421. If the raw seed's R stays ≈0.88240, the wall is not N-discretization and we learn to abandon that lever.
